study.title: Isaiah 6 The vision of the holy King, the call of the prophet, and the preserved remnant
study.overview: Isaiah 6 presents the decisive experience in which the prophet sees the Lord reigning in holiness, recognizes his own uncleanness, is purified on divine initiative and receives a difficult commission: to preach to a spiritually hardened people. The chapter ends with a severe but not hopeless judgment, for God preserves a holy seed, a remnant that survives disaster.

outline.title: The vision of the exalted Lord
outline.explanation: Isaiah sees the enthroned Lord, surrounded by heavenly beings who proclaim his holiness. The scene highlights the divine majesty and the reverberation of that glory in the whole temple.

outline.title: Conviction, purification and calling
outline.explanation: Faced with the holiness of God, Isaiah acknowledges his guilt and that of his people. A seraphim purifies him with a coal of the altar, and then the prophet responds to the divine call to be sent.

outline.title: Message of hardening and hope of the remnant
outline.explanation: Isaiah is sent to announce that the people will hear without understanding. The judgment will come to the devastation of the earth, but God will still preserve a small portion, compared to a trunk that remains after the court, the holy seed.

study.context: The chapter situates the vision in the year when King Uzziah died, marking a moment of political and spiritual transition. The notes suggest two possible readings: Isaiah may have received here his initial call, or his vocation may have been reaffirmed in a solemn way to introduce the next section of the book. In any case, the focus of the text is not in external historical details, but on the theological impact of the vision and commission.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God is absolutely holy, reigning above any human crisis. The right reaction before him is not self-confidence, but humble repentance, because human impurity makes the sinner unable to speak for himself before the Holy One. Purification comes from God, through a sacrificial action symbolized by the coal of the altar, which points to forgiveness as divine initiative. Then the prophetic vocation includes both the proclamation of truth and the proclamation of judgment on persistent resistance. The hardening described in the text does not deny human responsibility; it shows that repeatedly rejecting the word of God produces moral and spiritual blindness. Still, the chapter does not end in total destruction: God preserves a remnant, the holy seed, showing that judgment does not cancel his promises.

scholarViews.insight: Isaiah's vision functions as a turning point in his life and as a symbol of the need for conversion of the whole nation to fulfill his mission.
The glorious vision was given to confirm the faith of the prophet and also to affect his heart with reverence, preparing him for ministry.
The seraphim are presented as heavenly beings linked to fire, and their holiness highlights the depravity of the people who deserved to be consumed.

questions: What changes in our vision of God when we contemplate his holiness before thinking about our mission?
In which areas can I be listening to the word of God without really understanding it or obeying it?
How can the promise of a remnant sustain the faith when everything seems reduced to ruins?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader three practical answers: reverent worship, sincere confession, and readiness to obey. Set up time to recognize before God where your lips, thoughts, and desires are unclean; ask him to purify him before seeking to serve. Also examine whether there is persistent resistance to the word of God in your life, for the text warns that continuous refusal can harden the heart. Finally, serve with hope: even in times of loss, God preserves a holy seed and continues to act beyond what the eyes see.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not allow to define with certainty whether Isaiah 6 records his initial call or a solemn renewal of his commission; the two readings appear in the sources. There is also discussion in the notes about some textual details of the divine name, but this does not alter the main message of the chapter. The exact historical identification of the announced hardening is interpreted by the sources in relation to the people of the covenant and, in Christian reading, is also seen as a principle resumed in the ministry of Jesus, but this application remains interpretive.
